slides.title: The Graphics Pipeline
slides.notes: Open by positioning the pipeline as the object-order counterpart to ray tracing. The chapter is not only about hardware boxes; it is about the promises each stage makes to the next one. Ask students to watch for data that must survive coordinate changes, sampling choices, and visibility contests.

slides.title: Object-Order Rendering Changes The Loop Nest
slides.notes: Contrast the two mental loops carefully. Image-order rendering starts at a pixel and asks which scene objects matter there. Object-order rendering starts at a primitive and asks which pixels it can influence. That reversal explains why streaming geometry once can be fast, but also why visibility, aliasing, and edge ownership become pipeline responsibilities.

slides.title: The Pipeline Is A Chain Of Data Contracts
slides.notes: Use the diagram as a contract ledger rather than a simple flow chart. Each arrow should name what the next stage is allowed to assume. If an attribute, coordinate, or depth value is missing or represented inconsistently, the later stage cannot repair the mistake without doing different work.

slides.title: Vertex Processing Prepares Screen-Space Work
slides.notes: Emphasize that vertex processing is not merely multiplication by a matrix. It also decides which quantities are computed per vertex, which coordinate system is orthonormal enough for shading, and which homogeneous quantities must be preserved so the rasterizer can interpolate them correctly after projection.

slides.title: Rasterization Emits Fragments At Pixel Centers
slides.notes: Frame rasterization as two jobs performed together: enumerate covered sample locations and attach interpolated attributes to each resulting fragment. Pixel centers are a sampling convention, not a fact about geometry, so the class should see immediately why edge cases and antialiasing require additional policy.

slides.title: Barycentric Coordinates Are The Triangle Workhorse
slides.notes: Walk through the weights as a practical test and a practical interpolator. Nonnegative weights with sum one mean the sample is inside the triangle, and the same weights blend color, depth, texture coordinates after correction, or normals. This dual use is the reason triangles dominate pipeline design.

slides.title: Shared Edges Need Deterministic Ownership
slides.notes: This slide addresses a subtle bug students often miss. Adjacent triangles should tile a surface without gaps or double writes along their common boundary. A deterministic ownership convention assigns exact edge samples to one side, so the image does not depend on accidental draw order or floating point tie behavior.

slides.title: Perspective-Correct Interpolation Keeps Attributes Honest
slides.notes: Slow down on the algebraic idea without drowning the class in formulas. After perspective division, screen-linear interpolation is no longer world-linear. The repair is to interpolate homogeneous ratios such as u over w and one over w, then divide back at the fragment.

slides.title: Clipping Keeps Invalid Geometry Out Of Rasterization
slides.notes: Explain that clipping is a safety gate, not just an optimization. Primitives outside the view volume can be discarded, while primitives crossing a boundary must be trimmed so later division and rasterization operate on meaningful coordinates. The invariant is simple: every emitted vertex satisfies the view bounds.

slides.title: Fragment Processing And Blending Decide Pixel Winners
slides.notes: Connect this slide to the data contracts from the beginning. The rasterizer can create several fragments for the same pixel, but the framebuffer stores one resolved result per sample. Fragment processing supplies color and depth, while blending or depth testing determines whether the candidate becomes visible state.

slides.title: The Z-Buffer Localizes Hidden-Surface Decisions
slides.notes: Present the z-buffer as a deliberately local alternative to sorting geometry. It only solves the visibility question at pixels that are actually sampled, which is why it is so practical. The important teaching point is that the final visible color can be independent of primitive order when depths are well defined.

slides.title: Depth Precision Is A Near-Far Design Choice
slides.notes: Use the curve to make the near plane feel consequential. Perspective depth spends much more resolution near the eye than far away, so moving the near plane too close can make distant bins very coarse. Students should leave with the engineering rule: maximize near, minimize far, within scene requirements.

slides.title: Per-Vertex And Per-Fragment Shading Trade Cost For Detail
slides.notes: Keep the comparison tied to sampling frequency. Per-vertex shading is cheap when illumination changes slowly or geometry is dense enough, but it can miss a small highlight inside a large triangle. Per-fragment shading evaluates the lighting model where fragments actually land, at higher cost.

slides.title: Texture Mapping Adds An Image-Valued Attribute Source
slides.notes: Describe texture coordinates as another attribute contract. The primitive carries coordinates that identify where it lives in a texture domain, and the fragment shader performs a lookup to obtain material detail. This also previews why filtering and mipmaps matter in the later texture chapter.

slides.title: Antialiasing Separates Coverage Samples From Shading Samples
slides.notes: Use the split pixel diagram to distinguish visibility from color. Standard rasterization makes a binary decision at one sample location, which creates jagged edges. Supersampling estimates coverage by many samples, while multisampling reuses a color calculation but stores several coverage and depth decisions.

slides.title: Culling Saves Work With Conservative Tests
slides.notes: Make the performance logic explicit. Culling is valuable only when a cheap test discards work that cannot affect the framebuffer. View-volume culling can reject a whole bounded object conservatively, while backface culling relies on closed, consistently oriented surfaces whose rear-facing triangles are guaranteed to be hidden.

slides.title: Pipeline Debugging Means Checking Invariants
slides.notes: Close by turning the chapter into a debugging checklist. Students should be able to name the invariant at each stage: valid coordinates, single edge ownership, corrected interpolation, clipped primitives, depth winners, adequate sampling, and conservative culling. Those invariants are what make a renderer predictable.
